reasoning.Student A:
Because the mechanism is strategy-proof, truthful reporting is a dominant strategy: no possible misrepresentation of my preferences can yield a strictly better assignment regardless of how others rank schools. My true preference ordering is z > w > y > x, and I should therefore submit that ranking.

Although I have highest priority at w and y (w:1, y:1) and lower priority at z (z:2) and x (x:2), and many others favor y > x > w > z, these facts do not change the dominant strategy. Trying to rank a less-preferred school higher to game priorities cannot improve my outcome under a strategy-proof mechanism and may only risk getting a worse assignment. Thus I will report my true preferences.

My true preference ordering is w > y > z > x, so I should submit that order. Although many applicants favor y and x highly, and my priorities are w:2, x:1, y:2, z:1, strategic manipulation would not yield a better guaranteed outcome under a strategy-proof mechanism.

Because the mechanism is strategy-proof, it is a dominant strategy to report my true preferences; I cannot improve my outcome by misrepresenting them regardless of what others do. My true ordering is w > z > y > x, so I should submit that.

I note priorities: I have priority 3 at w and x, and 4 at y and z (1 is highest). Many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so y will be highly contested and, given my lower priority at y (4), I am less likely to get y than schools where I have higher priority. None of these facts change the conclusion from strategy-proofness: truthful ranking is best.
